question: For the first half of the 20th century, you could win an official Olympic medal without breaking a sweat. What kind of competition did you have to enter?
source_excerpt: Medal-awarding art competitions took place at the 1912, 1920, 1924, 1928, 1932, 1936, and 1948 Summer Games.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone assumes Olympic medals have always been for athletic feats. Learning that painters and poets once stood on the podium overturns that, and the 'without breaking a sweat' hint lets players reason their way to it.
extra.verification_notes: Art competitions awarded medals at the Olympics from 1912 to 1948; the IOC no longer tracks them in its medal tables, but they were official at the time (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Olympic_Games).

explanation: From 1912 to 1948 the Olympics awarded medals for sport-inspired painting, sculpture, music, literature and architecture. The founder of the modern Games, Pierre de Coubertin, even won a gold for a poem he entered under a pseudonym.

question: Why did the designer of the Olympic symbol choose exactly those colours: blue, yellow, black, green and red rings on a white background?
alternative_answers: Every country's flag has at least one
They cover all the world's flags
source_excerpt: reproduce the colours of every country, so every national flag contained at least one of these colours

extra.why_interesting: Players have seen the Olympic rings countless times and assume the colours are decorative or tied to specific continents. The real reason is clever and inclusive: between them, the colours appear in every country's flag. It can be reasoned out by picturing a few flags.
extra.verification_notes: Coubertin's stated rationale was that the rings' colours plus the white background cover every national flag of the time, which matches the claimed answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_symbols).

explanation: Pierre de Coubertin picked those six colours because every country's flag uses at least one of them, so every nation could see itself in the symbol. Many people think each colour stands for a continent, but no colour was ever officially tied to a particular continent.
